issues.legal_issue: A will is duly attested when the statutory requirements for the testator’s signature or acknowledgment and each attesting witness’s signature are met, even if the witnesses do not attest simultaneously.
material_facts: The testator signed the disputed will in the presence of both attesting witnesses, and each witness signed it in the testator’s presence.
The witnesses’ evidence supported that sequence, although they did not necessarily sign at the same time.
issues.conclusion: The will was not invalid merely because the attesting witnesses did not sign simultaneously; the evidence supported due attestation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 requires the testator to sign or acknowledge the will before each attesting witness and each witness to attest it in the testator’s presence; it does not require simultaneous attestation. Under Section 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, at least one attesting witness must be called to prove execution when available and capable of giving evidence. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma and the propositions set out in Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur.

predicates.will_attestation_proceeding: The dispute concerns whether a will was duly attested.
predicates.testator_signed_or_acknowledged_before_e: The testator signed the will before each attesting witness or personally acknowledged the testator’s signature to each witness.
predicates.each_witness_signed_in_testators_presenc: Each attesting witness signed the will while the testator was present.

issues.definition: When a will is in dispute and the testator signed or acknowledged it before each witness and each witness signed in the testator’s presence, the will is duly attested without requiring the witnesses to sign simultaneously.

issues.legal_issue: A later will is valid when its propounder proves due execution and the testator’s capacity and free will, and removes legitimate suspicion; the beneficiary’s participation or the exclusion of natural heirs does not alone invalidate it.
material_facts: The testator read and signed the later will in the presence of the attesting witnesses, who then signed in the testator’s presence.
The evidence supported that the testator was mentally and physically sound when the will was made.
The beneficiary and his family had cared for the testator and his wife, while the other sons had received property in earlier partitions and had not cared for their parents in their old age.
The challenge to the will relied on circumstances that the Court found unsupported by evidence or not sufficient, by themselves, to establish suspicion.
The beneficiary succeeded before the revenue authority on the basis of the later will, and the opposing son had not challenged that final order.
issues.conclusion: The propounder discharged the burden of proving the later will and dispelling legitimate suspicion. The High Court erred in rejecting it; the appeals were allowed and the trial court’s judgment was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 59 and 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and Sections 67 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 govern proof of a will and its attestation. The propounder must prove execution, the testator’s sound and disposing mind, and that the testator acted freely. Where legitimate suspicious circumstances exist, the propounder must remove them; the usual standard is the satisfaction of a prudent mind, not mathematical certainty. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B. N. Thimmajamma; Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur; Uma Devi Nambiar v. T. C. Sidhan; and Pentakota Satyanarayana v. Pentakota Seetharatnam. Excluding natural heirs, a beneficiary’s participation, and non-registration of a will do not, without more, establish invalidity.

rule.if: civil_will_validity_proceeding and will_execution_proved and testator_had_capacity and testator_acted_freely and legitimate_suspicions_removed

predicates.civil_will_validity_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the validity of a will in a civil dispute.
predicates.will_execution_proved: The propounder proved that the testator signed the will and that the attesting witnesses attested it as required.
predicates.testator_had_capacity: The evidence showed that the testator had a sound and disposing mind when making the will.
predicates.testator_acted_freely: The evidence showed that the testator made the will of the testator’s own free will.
predicates.legitimate_suspicions_removed: The propounder answered the circumstances that could reasonably cast doubt on the will, and the remaining objections were unsupported or insufficient to establish such doubt.

issues.definition: In a civil dispute over a will, proof of execution, capacity, and free choice, together with removal of legitimate suspicion, means the later will is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A duly proved later will that expresses the testator’s last wishes makes an inconsistent earlier will redundant without a separate express revocation.
material_facts: An earlier will distributed the testator’s share among his sons.
The later will bequeathed the testator’s share to one son and included a general statement cancelling any prior will.
The Court found the later will duly executed and proved.
issues.conclusion: Once the later will was duly proved, the earlier will became redundant because the later will represented the testator’s last wishes.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a later duly proved will represents the testator’s last wish and makes an inconsistent earlier will redundant; a separate categorical recital specifically identifying and cancelling the earlier will is not necessary for that result.

predicates.will_validity_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the effect or validity of competing wills.
predicates.earlier_will_exists: The testator made an earlier will dealing with the relevant property.
predicates.inconsistent_later_will_proved: The testator made a later will that was proved and made a different disposition of the relevant property.

issues.definition: Where competing wills are considered in a will dispute, proof of an inconsistent later will means the earlier will is redundant.
